title: Family seeks answers after teen dies in plunge into Niagara Gorge
subtitle: The family of 18-year-old Ryan Dube are seeking answers after the teen went over the retaining wall and plunged to his death into the Niagara Gorge.
article: Ryan Dube's family is looking for answers.

Less than 24 hours after Dube fell more than 30 metres to his death in the Niagara Gorge, his brothers and father stood at the retaining wall Dube went over, listening to the calm water and thinking about the 18-year-old "teddy bear" who they say would have given the shirt off his back to help someone in need.
They wiped their eyes and hugged each other, while two girls nearby held flowers to add to a makeshift memorial.
Something had to go terribly wrong, they say, for Dube to have jumped over this wall on River Rd., between Eastwood and Otter Sts.

The wall, which would have been below the 6-foot-2 Dube's waist, appears to be the only barrier between the road and the steep hill leading down to the gorge. Dube would have encountered rocks, trees, branches and other debris on his way down.

On Tuesday night, a Niagara Regional Police officer was chasing Dube on foot before the two went over the retaining wall, according to the Special Investigations Unit, which is probing the circumstances of Dube's death.

The officer, later identified by Niagara police as Const. Jacob Smits, was rescued at about 7:30 p.m. that night and transported to Hamilton General Hospital by air ambulance with a broken femur. He remained in hospital Wednesday.
More than an hour later, rescuers rappelled down the gorge and brought up Dube's body in a human-sized basket.

Police have released little information about the incident pending the SIU's investigation. The SIU is a provincial agency that investigates cases involving police where there has been death, serious injury or allegations of sexual assault.
Witnesses said they saw the young man running as he was pursued by an officer who jumped out of his cruiser and then continued the chase on foot.
"He didn't say a word. He just booked it," Logan Tremblay, who lives near the gorge, said of the officer.
"The kid went over the barrier, into the gorge and the cop went with him," he said.
Tremblay said there was no mistaking whether the officer jumped or tripped on the ledge.
"He full out hopped over and went out for the kid," he said.
"If they went a little bit to the right, or a little bit to the left, they would have been fine. They would have had enough land to stay put," said Tremblay.

Originally from St. Catharines, Dube was living at the Nightlight Youth Shelter, located a short walk away from where he plunged to his death. A worker there refused to comment about Dube Wednesday evening.
Dube had a troubled past and was in and out of jail, but was a good kid who was trying to change his lifestyle, his father, Jean Paul Dube said.
"He was making some good changes until this happened."
His brother, Patrick Gough, wanted Ryan to live with him instead of in a shelter. But his probation officer wouldn't allow it, the family said.
"He's been in and out of shelters all the time. He needed to be with his family," Gough said.
As a kid, Dube would jump off furniture and pretend to be Toy Story's Buzz Lightyear, his dad remembered.
Like his cartoon idol, Dube wanted to be a hero. He wanted to help youth as a police officer or social worker, warning kids to avoid the in-and-out-of-jail lifestyle he had.

Had he got the chance, his family believes Dube may have offered some of the same support to troubled kids that he offered his family members - a shoulder to cry on and an ear to listen whenever they had a problem.
Dube was three credits shy of finishing high school and moving on to his next challenge.
But he had trouble finding the support he needed to finish school and find a place to live away from drugs and fighting, his brother Patrick Gough said.
"No one wanted to help him. No school wanted to touch him."
But Ryan Dube was determined to get his life back in order because it's what would have made his late grandfather, Jean Marie Dube, proud.
Until he died of colon cancer three months ago, he was like a second father to Ryan Dube and his brothers.
"Every time he was down or Ryan had nowhere to go or no one to talk to, my grandfather was there for him and always supporting him," Gough said.
Now, Gough said, Ryan will be reunited with the grandfather he loved so dearly.
